incidents.title: Hungary: formation of the KESMA pro-government media foundation
incidents.summary: Owners aligned with Hungary's governing party donated 476 outlets into one non-profit foundation, KESMA. The government exempted the merger from the antitrust review that would normally apply to a combination of that size.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.what_happened: On November 29, 2018, the owners of 476 Hungarian outlets, including television channels, radio stations, news portals, newspapers and magazines, transferred them for no payment into a single non-profit body, the Central European Press and Media Foundation, known as KESMA. Most of these outlets had already been supportive of Prime Minister Viktor Orban's government; several had themselves been bought in earlier years by businesspeople close to the governing Fidesz party. Ordinarily a media combination of this scale would trigger a review by Hungary's competition authority to check its effect on media pluralism. The government instead declared the merger a matter of national interest and exempted it from that review by decree. KESMA's outlets now make up a large share of Hungary's total media market, alongside the country's state broadcaster.
incidents.stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Hungary's press freedom organization Reporters Without Borders later said the government-aligned foundation and state broadcasting together dominate about eighty percent of the national media market, crowding out independent competitors for advertising and audience.
incidents.status: Sustained; KESMA continued to operate as of the sources reviewed.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not give the government's stated reason for exempting the merger from competition review.
incidents.outcome_note: The merger was completed and the exemption was not reported as reversed in the sources reviewed.

claims.value: 476 outlets donated to KESMA
claims.statement: The number of outlets folded into the new foundation.
claims.evidence_quote: In December, the owners of 476 progovernment titles donated their outlets to a new non-profit entity called KESMA for free; the merger was exempted from antitrust review on "national interest" grounds.

claims.statement: RSF's characterization of the state broadcaster over the same period.
claims.evidence_quote: public broadcasting was turned into a propaganda machine

incidents.ladder_note: Owners surrendered 476 outlets into one government-aligned foundation, exempted by decree from antitrust review; United States funding pressure has cut money and licenses but has not required owners to give up outlets.

incidents.title: Hungary: editor fired and staff resign at Index.hu
incidents.summary: Index.hu, Hungary's most-read independent news site, fired editor-in-chief Szabolcs Dull weeks after he warned that a change in ownership threatened its independence. Most of the newsroom resigned within days.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.what_happened: In March 2020, businessman Miklos Vaszily, who had previously run outlets aligned with Prime Minister Viktor Orban's government, gained an indirect stake in the company that sells advertising for Index.hu, Hungary's largest independent news site. On June 22, 2020, editor-in-chief Szabolcs Dull published a public letter, co-signed by most of the newsroom, saying the site's independence was in danger. Index.hu added a public indicator it called a barometer to track the threat. On July 22, 2020, company leadership fired Dull. Two days later, more than seventy of the outlet's roughly ninety journalists resigned, saying they could no longer guarantee independent coverage. Many of the departing staff went on to found a new outlet, Telex.hu, later that year. Index.hu continued operating under new ownership and editorial leadership.
incidents.stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: The mass resignation removed most of the reporting staff Index.hu had built over two decades and shifted its ownership toward people described in the sources reviewed as close to the government.
incidents.status: Sustained; Dull's dismissal was not reversed and Index.hu continued under its new ownership.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not give the company's stated reason for dismissing Dull.
incidents.outcome_note: Dull's dismissal stood and the outlet continued under its changed ownership; the sources reviewed do not report a reversal.

claims.value: Dull dismissed July 22, 2020
claims.statement: Confirmation of the firing date.
claims.evidence_quote: Szabolcs Dull was dismissed by company leadership in July.

claims.value: More than 70 staff resign
claims.statement: Scale of the newsroom departure.
claims.evidence_quote: Editorial board of Index and more than 70 staff members resign

claims.value: Ownership passed to pro-government circles
claims.statement: Freedom House's description of the buyer.
claims.evidence_quote: Index.hu was sold to progovernment business circles

incidents.ladder_note: An editor was fired and most of a ninety-person newsroom resigned after a government-linked businessman gained influence over the outlet's ownership; United States funding pressure has not removed an editor through an ownership change.

incidents.title: Poland: state oil company Orlen buys the Polska Press newspaper group
incidents.summary: Poland's state-controlled oil company PKN Orlen completed the purchase of Polska Press, a group of 20 regional newspapers reaching millions of readers, from its German owner, over objections from Poland's human rights commissioner.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.what_happened: PKN Orlen, an oil and gas company majority owned by the Polish state, announced on December 7, 2020, that it would buy Polska Press, a group of 20 regional daily newspapers and about 120 local weeklies and websites reaching an estimated 17.4 million readers, from Germany's Verlagsgruppe Passau. Poland's national human rights commissioner, Adam Bodnar, warned in March 2021 that state control over the group could let officials influence editorial boards. Orlen completed the acquisition in April 2021 and installed a new management team. Some journalists at member papers, including Polska Times, said their day-to-day assignments had not changed immediately but that they feared future interference. On February 10, 2021, dozens of independent Polish outlets, including national broadcasters, staged a one-day protest against a separate proposed advertising tax, running the message "Media without choice" instead of normal programming, a protest that took place against the backdrop of the Orlen deal.
incidents.stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Polska Press journalists described uncertainty about their outlets' editorial direction once a state-controlled company held ownership, even before any specific change in coverage was reported.
incidents.status: Sustained as of the sources reviewed.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not report whether Orlen changed the editorial line of specific Polska Press titles after the sale closed.
incidents.outcome_note: The acquisition closed and was not reported as reversed in the sources reviewed.

incidents.title: Turkiye: court installs trustees at Zaman newspaper
incidents.summary: An Istanbul court put Turkiye's best-selling newspaper, Zaman, and its parent company under trustees after ruling it supported a group the government called a terrorist organization. Police used tear gas on a crowd that gathered in support.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.what_happened: On March 4, 2016, an Istanbul court ruled that Feza Media Group, publisher of the newspapers Zaman and Today's Zaman and the Cihan news agency, supported a movement led by the exiled cleric Fethullah Gulen that Turkiye's government had labeled a terrorist organization. The court ordered the company placed under court-appointed trustees, who took control of its board, servers and archives and blocked existing journalists' access to their own systems. Police used tear gas and water cannons to disperse a crowd that had gathered outside Zaman's Istanbul office in support of the paper. Within days, the new management removed critical stories from the paper's history and installed an editorial line supportive of the government; the paper's foreign editor and other senior staff were dismissed. Today's Zaman continued for several more months before all Feza-linked outlets were permanently closed by a state-of-emergency decree following the failed coup attempt of July 2016.
incidents.stated_justification: "the new administration does not want any stories that were 'critical of Turkey'"
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Journalists said the paper reversed its editorial line within days and that the takeover was part of a broader effort described by one ousted editor as aimed at every independent voice, not only Zaman.
incidents.status: Sustained until the outlets were later closed entirely by decree in July 2016.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not include the trustees' own account of why specific staff were dismissed.
incidents.outcome_note: Editorial control was not restored to the original owners; the outlets were later shut down entirely under a separate July 2016 decree.

claims.evidence_quote: an Istanbul court on Friday ruled that Zaman and Today's Zaman support an alleged terrorist organization

claims.evidence_quote: police used tear gas and water cannons against journalists and protesters who gathered to support them

claims.evidence_quote: the new managers took over the dailies' servers and archives and blocked journalists' access

claims.evidence_quote: Erdoğan is killing journalism. It's not just about Zaman and Today's Zaman. Everyone is targeted.

incidents.ladder_note: A court replaced a newspaper's board and editors with trustees days after a hearing without the company's lawyers present; United States funding pressure has not removed an outlet's management by court order.

incidents.title: Turkiye: Dogan Holding sells its media outlets to Demiroren
incidents.summary: Turkiye's largest independent media group, including the newspaper Hurriyet and the broadcaster CNN Turk, was sold to the Demiroren conglomerate, a buyer with ties to the governing party, for a reported 1.1 billion dollars.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.what_happened: Dogan Holding, one of Turkiye's largest conglomerates, announced on March 21, 2018, that it would sell its media assets, including the newspapers Hurriyet and Posta and the television channels Kanal D and CNN Turk, to Demiroren Holding for a reported 1.1 billion dollars. Dogan's outlets had been among the few remaining large media companies not aligned with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's government, though the group had already softened its coverage under years of tax disputes and legal pressure. Demiroren had a record of changing coverage after previous purchases: when it bought the newspapers Milliyet and Vatan from Dogan in 2011, both switched to a government-supportive editorial line. Journalists said the sale would place Turkiye's mass media even more directly under pro-government ownership, since Demiroren's chairman had personal and business ties to Erdogan.
incidents.stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Journalists covering the sale said it would extend pro-government ownership over the last major independent broadcaster and newspaper group, following the same pattern seen at Demiroren's earlier acquisitions.
incidents.status: Sustained; the sale closed as announced.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not give the sale's final confirmed price beyond the reported figure.
incidents.outcome_note: The sale closed and was not reported as reversed in the sources reviewed.

claims.statement: The CPJ chronicle's description of the announced sale.
claims.evidence_quote: Doğan Holding, one of Turkey's largest conglomerates, on March 21 announced that it would sell its media assets to the pro-government Demirören Holding.

claims.evidence_quote: Two of Turkey's top-selling newspapers, Hurriyet and Posta, and its main entertainment and news channels, Kanal D and CNN Turk, would be included in the sale, the news reports said.

incidents.ladder_note: Turkiye's largest remaining independent newspaper and broadcast group was sold to a buyer with ties to the president, following two prior purchases that turned pro-government; United States pressure on owners has not produced a forced sale of this kind.

incidents.title: Russia: CBC/Radio-Canada bureau closed and journalists' visas cancelled
incidents.summary: Russian authorities ordered the Canadian broadcaster CBC/Radio-Canada's Moscow bureau closed and cancelled its journalists' visas and accreditation, part of a wave of expulsions and non-renewals of foreign correspondents after the invasion of Ukraine.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.what_happened: On May 18, 2022, Russian authorities moved to close the Moscow bureau of CBC/Radio-Canada, Canada's public broadcaster, and cancelled the visas and accreditation of its correspondents there, ending the outlet's ability to report from inside the country. The action came three months into Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, during a period in which Russia also blocked the websites of the BBC's Russian service, Germany's Deutsche Welle and other outlets, and later denied visa renewals to correspondents from the Netherlands and Finland and expelled two German journalists. Canada had imposed sanctions on Russian officials and state media figures over the invasion, and Russian officials described several of these press-related measures as reciprocal steps against countries that had sanctioned Russia or its state broadcasters.
incidents.stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: The closure ended CBC's ability to report from inside Russia during the war, joining several other Western outlets whose correspondents lost accreditation or visas over the same period.
incidents.status: Sustained; the bureau remained closed in the sources reviewed.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not give Russia's specific stated reason for acting against CBC's bureau on that date.
incidents.outcome_note: The bureau closure and visa cancellations were not reported as reversed in the sources reviewed.

incidents.title: Ethiopia: Economist correspondent Tom Gardner expelled
incidents.summary: Ethiopia's media regulator revoked The Economist correspondent Tom Gardner's press accreditation and gave him 48 hours to leave the country, citing unspecified conduct, almost a year after expelling a New York Times reporter.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.what_happened: On May 13, 2022, Ethiopia's Media Authority revoked the press accreditation of Tom Gardner, a correspondent for The Economist who had reported from the country for several years, and ordered him to leave within 48 hours. The authority said Gardner had failed to meet unspecified standards of conduct for journalists; weeks earlier, in March 2022, officials had accused him of posting information on social media that was not properly sourced or supported by government authorities. Gardner's expulsion came almost a year after Ethiopian authorities similarly expelled New York Times correspondent Simon Marks in May 2021, during the country's civil war with forces from the Tigray region. The Economist said Gardner's reporting on Ethiopia had been professional and unbiased.
incidents.stated_justification: "failed to live to [the] standards of conduct for journalists"
incidents.effect_on_reporting: The expulsion removed one of the few remaining Western correspondents reporting on Ethiopia's civil war from inside the country, following a similar expulsion the year before.
incidents.status: Closed; Gardner left the country within the 48-hour deadline.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not specify which standards of conduct the authority said Gardner failed to meet.
incidents.outcome_note: The expulsion was carried out and was not reported as reversed in the sources reviewed.

claims.value: Authority cites failure to meet conduct standards
claims.statement: The regulator's stated reason for revoking accreditation.
claims.evidence_quote: failed to live to [the] standards of conduct for journalists

claims.evidence_quote: Gardner's reporting on Ethiopia has been professional, unbiased and often courageous.

incidents.title: Nicaragua: freelance correspondent detained and deported after online campaign
incidents.summary: A coordinated online campaign accused freelance correspondent Carl David Goette-Luciak of being a foreign agent and circulated his home address, after which he was detained and deported from Nicaragua in September 2018.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.what_happened: Beginning September 16, 2018, dozens of social media accounts, some appearing automated and posting nearly identical messages within minutes of one another, began sharing photographs and videos of Carl David Goette-Luciak, a United States-Austrian freelance journalist who had reported from Nicaragua on protests against President Daniel Ortega's government for outlets including The Guardian and The Washington Post. The posts accused him of working for the Central Intelligence Agency and of trying to destabilize the country, and some included his home address; other users called for him to be captured and handed to police, or expelled. Some of the accounts sharing the material were linked to government-affiliated organizations. Goette-Luciak was later detained and deported from Nicaragua that September.
incidents.stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: The campaign and subsequent deportation removed one of the few foreign freelance correspondents then covering Nicaragua's protest movement for major English-language outlets.
incidents.status: Closed; Goette-Luciak was deported and did not return to report from Nicaragua in the period covered by the sources reviewed.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not name the government office responsible for the deportation order.
incidents.outcome_note: The deportation was not reported as reversed; the sources reviewed record at least 50 Nicaraguan journalists in exile by mid-2019.

incidents.title: Turkiye: Dutch freelance journalist Ans Boersma deported
incidents.summary: Turkish authorities detained Dutch freelance journalist Ans Boersma while she tried to renew her residence permit in Istanbul and deported her the next day, citing an alleged link to a Syrian armed group that the Netherlands said it had never been asked about.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.what_happened: On January 16, 2019, Turkish authorities took Ans Boersma, a Dutch freelance journalist based in Istanbul, into custody while she attempted to renew her residence permit at the city's Foreigners' Office. She was held overnight at a police station and deported the next day, January 17, without being allowed to return to her home to collect belongings. Turkish officials linked the deportation to an allegation that Boersma had ties to Jabhat al-Nusra, a Syrian armed group. The Dutch government said Turkey had made no request for her detention, expulsion or extradition and that it had not been consulted about the allegation before she was removed. Boersma had reported on Turkiye and Syria for several years before the deportation.
incidents.stated_justification: "The Netherlands told Turkey that the reporter, who was deported today, had links to Jabhat al-Nusra."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: The deportation removed a working foreign correspondent from the country on an allegation her own government said it had not been asked to confirm.
incidents.status: Closed; Boersma was deported and did not return to report from Turkiye in the period covered by the sources reviewed.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not include the evidence Turkish authorities cited for the Jabhat al-Nusra allegation.
incidents.outcome_note: The deportation was not reported as reversed in the sources reviewed.

incidents.title: India: journalist Aatish Taseer's overseas citizenship revoked
incidents.summary: India's government cancelled writer and journalist Aatish Taseer's Overseas Citizen of India status months after he wrote a Time magazine cover story critical of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, citing his father's Pakistani nationality.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.what_happened: In May 2019, Time magazine published a cover story by writer and journalist Aatish Taseer that was critical of Prime Minister Narendra Modi ahead of that year's general election. On August 13, 2019, India's Home Ministry sent Taseer a notice threatening to revoke his Overseas Citizen of India status, a form of long-term immigration status that lets people of Indian origin live and work in the country without a visa. The ministry said Taseer was ineligible for the status because his father, the Pakistani politician Salmaan Taseer, was a Pakistani national, and Pakistani nationals cannot hold it. On November 7, 2019, the government made the cancellation official. Taseer disputed the notice, said he did not hold Pakistani citizenship, and said he believed the action was linked to his criticism of the Modi government.
incidents.stated_justification: "his father was a Pakistani national, and Pakistani nationals are not eligible for such status"
incidents.effect_on_reporting: The cancellation ended Taseer's ability to enter India on his Overseas Citizen status, restricting a foreign-based journalist's access to the country whose government he had written about.
incidents.status: Closed; the cancellation was made official in November 2019.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not report whether Taseer obtained an alternative visa to enter India afterward.
incidents.outcome_note: The cancellation was carried out and was not reported as reversed in the sources reviewed.

claims.statement: The government's stated legal basis for the cancellation.
claims.evidence_quote: Taseer was "ineligible" for such citizenship

incidents.title: Myanmar: military cuts mobile internet after seizing power
incidents.summary: After seizing power on February 1, 2021, Myanmar's military cut mobile data service nationwide, leaving reporters in rural townships and Rakhine State unable to send news and blocking large areas from outside communication for months.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.what_happened: On February 1, 2021, Myanmar's military, led by Commander-in-Chief Min Aung Hlaing, seized power from the elected government and detained its leaders. In the weeks that followed, the military ordered mobile internet providers to cut data service, first intermittently and then for extended stretches, across large parts of the country. Reporters for local outlets said the blackout made it difficult or impossible to send news out of affected areas; one editor said reporters in different townships found it very hard to file their stories once mobile data was blocked. In Rakhine State, in the country's west, journalists described a total blockage of mobile data across northern cities and rural areas for months. The shutdown compounded restrictions the military had already placed on domestic media licenses and on journalists' movement.
incidents.stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Local reporters said the shutdown of mobile data made it very difficult to send news out of affected townships, cutting off some regions from outside coverage for months at a time.
incidents.status: Ongoing as of the source reviewed, published in May 2021.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not give an exact date when service was restored in each affected region.
incidents.outcome_note: As of the May 2021 source, mobile data remained cut in parts of the country, including large areas of Rakhine State.

claims.evidence_quote: Since mobile internet usage [was] blocked by the military junta, our reporters in different townships have found it really difficult to send their news stories

incidents.title: China: citizen journalist Zhang Zhan imprisoned for Wuhan reporting

incidents.issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.

incidents.title: Eritrea: independent press closed and journalists jailed without trial

incidents.title: Russia: outlet fined $338,000 under the foreign agents law
incidents.summary: A Moscow court fined the magazine The New Times 22.3 million rubles, about $338,000, for a paperwork lapse under Russia's foreign agents law, a sum its editor said was designed to force the outlet to close.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.what_happened: On October 26, 2018, a Moscow court ordered the magazine The New Times to pay 22.3 million rubles, about $338,000, for failing to provide financial information required under Russia's foreign agents law, which requires organizations that receive funding from abroad to register and report on their finances or face penalties. The New Times had already been financially strained, having stopped producing a print edition in June 2017 for lack of money. Its editor said she had in fact reported the required information correctly to the proper authorities and said she would appeal the fine. CPJ said the fine was clearly intended to cripple the outlet and amounted to a serious threat to what remained of press freedom in Russia, since a sum of that size threatened the magazine's ability to keep operating at all.
incidents.stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: A fine of that size, imposed on an outlet already unable to afford printing, threatened to end The New Times' operations entirely rather than simply penalize a specific story.

incidents.title: Malta: minister orders reporter's bank account frozen
incidents.summary: A month after journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia published reporting on members of Malta's government, the economy minister had her bank account frozen, one of dozens of legal actions she faced before she was killed in a car bombing in October 2017.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.what_happened: Daphne Caruana Galizia, Malta's best-known investigative journalist, published reporting in January 2017 that included compromising information about members of Prime Minister Joseph Muscat's government. The following month, February 2017, Malta's economy minister had her bank account frozen, an administrative order that cut off her access to her own funds while she continued reporting. The freeze came during a period in which Caruana Galizia faced dozens of civil defamation suits from government officials and businesspeople she had reported on, filed in Malta and abroad, which press freedom groups later described as an attempt to exhaust her financially and legally rather than to win any single case. Caruana Galizia was killed in a car bombing outside her home on October 16, 2017, while several of the suits against her remained pending.
incidents.stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: The frozen account was one of many financial and legal pressures Caruana Galizia faced in the months before her killing, alongside dozens of separate lawsuits from officials and businesspeople named in her reporting.
incidents.status: Unresolved as of her killing in October 2017; legal actions against her family continued afterward.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not state when or whether the freeze on her account was lifted before her death.
incidents.outcome_note: The source reviewed does not report the freeze being lifted before her 2017 killing; five people were later sentenced over the killing itself between 2022 and 2026, while defamation suits continued against her family.

incidents.title: Kazakhstan: fabricated copyright complaints used against journalists
incidents.summary: An investigation found paid services in Kazakhstan filing fabricated copyright complaints, impersonating global brands, to get social media platforms to remove journalists' accounts and posts, alongside criminal prosecutions of the press.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.what_happened: CPJ reported on August 20, 2026, that journalists in Kazakhstan faced a pattern of legal and platform-based pressure that included prosecutions, professional bans and what it called spurious copyright claims. One case involved journalist Azamat Omarov, whose YouTube and Instagram accounts were repeatedly removed or blocked based on copyright complaints CPJ said appeared fabricated. An investigation by the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, cited in the CPJ report, found an underground market of agencies charging up to $5,000 to file false copyright complaints against journalists, sometimes using email addresses that impersonated global brands including L'Oreal and Giorgio Armani. Diana Okremova of the Legal Media Center said platforms needed to account for Kazakhstan's political context before acting on a single complaint against a journalist or public figure.
incidents.stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: The fabricated complaints removed journalists' social media accounts and posts without any court proceeding, using platform copyright rules as a substitute for a lawsuit.

incidents.title: Russia: new laws penalize online "fake news" and "disrespecting authorities"
incidents.summary: Russia's parliament passed laws letting courts jail and fine people, including journalists, for posting information the government alone judges to be false, or for statements found to disrespect officials or state symbols online.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.what_happened: On March 7, 2019, Russia's State Duma passed legislation permitting courts to jail and fine people who use the internet to spread what the law calls "fake news" or to disrespect government officials and state symbols, including President Vladimir Putin. Under the fake-news provisions, individuals, including journalists, could be fined up to 100,000 rubles, and companies up to 500,000 rubles, for posting unverified information that authorities determine threatens someone's life, health or property, or threatens mass public disorder. Separately, people found guilty of posting what courts call indecent statements about the government could face up to 15 days in administrative detention, with fines rising to 200,000 rubles and repeat violations carrying additional jail time. CPJ said the legislation was clearly aimed at tightening state control over independent media and pressuring journalists toward self-censorship.
incidents.stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: The law gave authorities a standing legal tool to fine or briefly jail journalists and ordinary internet users over reporting or commentary the government alone determined to be false or disrespectful, without a specific factual dispute needing to be argued in court beforehand.
incidents.status: Sustained; the laws remained in force and were later expanded during the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not report how many people were fined or jailed under the law in its first year.
incidents.outcome_note: The laws were enacted and were later expanded in March 2022 to include prison terms of up to 15 years for wartime 'fakes.'

incidents.title: Russia: independent outlet Meduza designated a 'foreign agent'
incidents.summary: Russia's Justice Ministry labeled the independent news site Meduza and outlet PASMI "foreign agents," a status requiring constant public disclosure, quarterly reports and audits, and carrying up to two years in prison for noncompliance, which Meduza said would destroy its advertising business.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.what_happened: On April 23, 2021, Russia's Justice Ministry added the independent news site Meduza, which is based in Latvia and widely read inside Russia, and the outlet PASMI to its register of "foreign agents." The designation, created under a law expanded over several years to cover media organizations and individuals, requires labeled outlets to mark every piece of content with a foreign agent notice, provide a legal representative inside Russia, file quarterly financial reports and semi-annual activity reports, and undergo annual audits. People working for a foreign agent outlet who fail to comply can face up to two years in prison. Meduza's editor said the label would deprive the outlet of the ability to fully practice journalism inside Russia and would destroy its business, since advertisers would avoid being associated with a designated outlet. CPJ called on Russia to stop labeling independent outlets as foreign agents.
incidents.stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Meduza's editor said the label would cut off the outlet's advertising revenue and constrain its ability to operate as a normal news organization inside Russia, years before Russia banned it outright in 2023.
incidents.status: Sustained; the designation remained in place and Russia later outlawed Meduza entirely.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not give the Justice Ministry's specific stated reason for designating Meduza on that date.
incidents.outcome_note: The designation was not reversed; Russia later declared Meduza an 'undesirable organization' and outlawed it entirely.

incidents.title: Egypt: media law used to fine and block news site al-Mashhad
incidents.summary: Under a 2018 law that treats any social media account with more than 5,000 followers as a media outlet, Egypt's media regulator fined news site al-Mashhad and ordered internet providers to block it for spreading what it called false news.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.what_happened: Egypt's Law No. 180 of 2018 applies to every online and offline media outlet and, separately, to any social media account with more than 5,000 followers, treating such accounts as media outlets subject to regulation by the state's Supreme Council for Media Regulation. The law bans content the council judges to be false news, defamatory, obscene, or a threat to national security, with violators facing fines of up to 250,000 Egyptian pounds and having their websites blocked. On March 22, 2019, the council fined the news site al-Mashhad 50,000 Egyptian pounds and ordered Egyptian internet providers to block the site for six months. Al-Mashhad appealed, and on April 7 the council reduced the block to one month starting from the appeal date, but the site remained inaccessible inside Egypt as of May 7, 2019, according to the source reviewed.
incidents.stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: The law let a state regulator fine and block a news site inside the country over content it alone judged false, without the matter going before an ordinary court first.
incidents.status: Unresolved; al-Mashhad remained blocked in Egypt as of the date given in the source reviewed.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not report whether the block was lifted after May 7, 2019.
incidents.outcome_note: Al-Mashhad's website was still inaccessible in Egypt as of May 7, 2019, the last date given in the source reviewed.

incidents.title: Vietnam: Decree 72 restricts blogs to personal information
incidents.summary: Vietnam's Decree 72 took effect in September 2013, barring bloggers and social media users from linking to or reposting news from press organizations or foreign government websites, restricting them to sharing personal information only.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.what_happened: Vietnam's government issued Decree 72 in 2013, and it took effect on September 1, 2013, broadly prohibiting Vietnamese bloggers and internet users from linking to or reposting news from press organizations or information from foreign government websites, restricting personal blogs and social media accounts to sharing personal information only. The decree did not specify how global internet companies would be penalized if they refused to cooperate with government orders to identify bloggers who violated it or restrict their posts. A coalition of internet companies, the Asia Internet Coalition, said the decree would negatively affect Vietnam's internet economy and discourage businesses from operating in the country. A Vietnamese Ministry of Information official denied the decree amounted to a ban, saying the government had never stopped people from sharing information or linking to news from other websites.
incidents.stated_justification: "We never ban people from sharing information or linking news from websites."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: The decree gave authorities a legal basis to treat ordinary sharing or reposting of news articles online as a violation, adding to prosecutions Vietnam had already brought against individual bloggers over their reporting.
incidents.status: Sustained as of the source reviewed.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not report how many people were penalized specifically under Decree 72 in its first years.
incidents.outcome_note: The decree remained in force and was not reported as reversed in the source reviewed.

incidents.title: Belarus: Deutsche Welle and other outlets labeled 'extremist'
incidents.summary: A Minsk court declared all output from German broadcaster Deutsche Welle "extremist," alongside a local newspaper and a Russian blogger's videos, making it a crime to produce, store or share the labeled material, as a former correspondent was jailed the same week.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.what_happened: On March 3, 2022, a Minsk district court sentenced Aleh Hruzdzilovich, a former correspondent for Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, to a year and a half in prison over his participation in three protests in 2020. Days later, on March 9, 2022, Minsk's Central District Court declared all information products of Deutsche Welle, Germany's public broadcaster, to be extremist material, effectively banning the outlet inside Belarus. The same order labeled the independent newspaper Regionalnaya Gazeta and videos by Russian blogger Yuriy Dud extremist as well, bringing the total number of outlets Belarus had designated extremist to 20. Under Belarusian law, anyone convicted of producing, storing or sharing material labeled extremist can be fined up to 960 rubles or detained for up to 15 days; Belarus's information ministry separately warned that even subscribing to a labeled outlet's Telegram channel could lead to prosecution.
incidents.stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: The designation made it a punishable offense inside Belarus to read, store or share Deutsche Welle's reporting, cutting off a foreign broadcaster's audience by criminalizing the audience's own conduct rather than the broadcaster's.
incidents.status: Sustained as of the source reviewed.
incidents.what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not report whether the designation was later narrowed or lifted.
incidents.outcome_note: The designation brought the total number of outlets labeled extremist in Belarus to 20 and was not reported as reversed.
